title: The Legal Thriller from Gardner to Grisham
finding: Historical overview (book) of the legal thriller as a crime-fiction subgenre largely written by legal professionals; per the author it typically uses the trial as the suspense-creating background for presenting legal issues, from corporate conflicts to private concerns, 'in a dramatic but highly informed manner'.
why_for_us: Supports framing 'Komputerku' as a legal thriller where suspense comes from an informed legal issue, not from violence; the notarial act (deed signing) can play the structural role the trial plays in the classic form.

title: Lawyer as critic: analysing the legal thriller through the works of John Grisham, Erle Stanley Gardner and Harper Lee
finding: Essay arguing that Gardner, Lee and Grisham present lawyer protagonists as critics of the law and of the legal systems they belong to, against legal scholars who read these works as merely critical of lawyers.
why_for_us: A notary hero can be both insider and critic of the system (e.g. noticing where procedure fails a vulnerable client) without the series attacking the profession its audience belongs to.

title: Justice Denoted: The Legal Thriller in American, British, and Continental Courtroom Literature
finding: Annotated bibliography (book) of legal-suspense fiction, plays, film and TV scripts across American, British and continental traditions; per the author the selection deliberately rejects labels that reduce the legal thriller to a subgenre of mystery fiction.
why_for_us: Reference for finding continental (civil-law) examples to benchmark against; also a reminder that the 'legal thriller' label can cover non-mystery suspense such as a contested transaction.

title: John Grisham: A Critical Companion
finding: Critical companion (book) explaining how Grisham's legal thriller evolved from the thriller tradition and borrowed from heroic romance, gothic, crime and detective fiction; the author claims the legal thriller was then the most popular genre in American fiction.
why_for_us: Grisham's template (young professional, powerful institution, hidden paper trail) maps onto a notary office story; heroic-romance borrowing suggests a clear protector role for the notary toward Irena.

title: 6. Spy fiction, the thriller and legal drama
finding: Chapter in 'Crime Fiction: A Very Short Introduction' that places legal drama alongside spy fiction and the thriller as distinct branches of crime writing; the abstract traces the thriller lineage (Fleming, Le Carré, Forsyth) before turning to legal drama.
why_for_us: Useful as a compact genre map for the writers' room: legal drama shares the thriller's engine (threat, time pressure, concealed information) even when the threat is a fraud rather than a killing.

title: Языковые средства создания атмосферы напряжения в произведениях жанра триллер (на примере романов Дж. Гришэма и М. Стюарт)
finding: Russian-language linguistic study of suspense technique in Grisham's legal thrillers and Mary Stewart's romantic suspense; per the authors suspense is built with universal devices such as comparative tropes, imagery and semantic repetition.
why_for_us: Concrete verbal tools (repetition of a key phrase, a recurring image such as a date or seal) can carry suspense in a 60-90 s script with very little action.

title: See You in Court (3). The American Genre Explosion from the Late 1980s: The Men
finding: Chapter noting that both the American legal trade and the legal thriller are male-dominated (per counts from White's compilation) and citing survey statistics that 'mystery, thriller, and crime' made up a large share (47 per cent in one July 2015 survey) of books read.
why_for_us: Indicates a broad existing appetite for the genre; a female-led notary office and a female client (Irena) can differentiate the series from the male-dominated tradition.

title: Law in Film: Globalizing the Hollywood Courtroom Drama
finding: Essay on the courtroom drama as a prominent, mostly Hollywood film genre in which essential parts of the story take place in court; the authors argue these films strongly influence the public's concept of justice even though few accurately reflect legal reality; the title frames this as the globalisation of the Hollywood courtroom drama.
why_for_us: Polish viewers (including notary staff) carry Hollywood courtroom expectations; the series should deliberately replace jury-and-objection imagery with the real continental setting of a notary's desk and deed reading.

title: The Social Issue Courtroom Drama as an Expression of American Popular Culture
finding: Essay distinguishing two varieties of the American courtroom picture, the problem film in the guise of a legal drama and the social-issue trial movie, which per the author merge into a category marked by liberal stances and humanitarian attitudes toward excesses of rigid law.
why_for_us: A season-long social issue (protecting elderly sellers from well-meaning or predatory relatives) can give the episodic cases a shared moral spine, as social-issue courtroom films do.

title: Law and Justice as Seen on TV
finding: Book examining the surge of law-related TV programming, fiction and non-fiction, since live televised trials became media events, linking media history, legal policy and the political shift to the right.
why_for_us: Background on why legal TV is popular and politically charged; reminds the team that even a short legal series makes implicit claims about who protects citizens.

title: Of Legal Roulette and Eccentric Clients - Contemporary TV Legal Drama as (Post-)Postmodern Public Sphere
venue: Qucosa (Saxon State and University Library Dresden)
finding: Essay arguing that TV courtroom drama exploits the theatricality of trials to invite audiences to deliberate on social or political issues negotiated in courtroom plots, and that contemporary shows add a self-reflexive dimension.
why_for_us: Each episode can end on an open question for viewers ('whose will is this?') that invites deliberation, since the genre already trains audiences to weigh competing versions.

title: Passing judgement: the ‘double trial structure’ of four Hollywood legal dramas
finding: Book chapter on a 'double trial structure' in four Hollywood legal dramas; the OpenAlex record has no abstract, so only the title is known.
why_for_us: Title suggests a structure in which a formal hearing runs alongside an informal judgement of characters, a pattern that fits a deed-signing scene that is also a test of the son's credibility.

title: A History of Representations of Justice: Coincident Preoccupations of Law and Film
finding: Essay arguing that the American trial and cinema share epistemological tendencies: both claim authoritative knowledge based on observable phenomena and are preoccupied with sustaining the authority of visual perception; the trial film is as old as cinema itself.
why_for_us: Supports making the visual inspection of a document (signature, date, seal, ID photo) the decisive 'evidence on screen' moment in each episode.

title: Television's “New” Feminism: Prime-Time Representations of Women and Victimization
finding: Essay on Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, which per the authors blends a focus on sexual assault with the historically masculine detective genre; it integrates feminist insights but its depictions of women criminals and feminine qualities remain problematic.
why_for_us: A cautionary model for portraying a vulnerable elderly woman: centre Irena's agency and avoid reducing her to a victim while the notary protects her will.

title: The Detective as Reader: Narrativity and Reading Concepts in Detective Fiction
finding: Essay arguing that classical detective fiction thematizes narrativity itself: its point is reconstructing a hidden or lost story (the crime) through reading signs, so the detective acts as a model reader.
why_for_us: The notary is a professional reader of documents; each episode can stage reconstruction of the 'hidden story' behind a deed (who drafted it, when, under whose pressure) through reading its signs.

title: The Typology of Detective Fiction (1966)
finding: Reprint of Todorov's structuralist essay classifying detective fiction into sub-types that develop according to their own rules; the abstract presents it as a structuralist approach in which certain apparently insignificant features can be codified by type.
why_for_us: Lets the team choose deliberately between a whodunit form (reconstruct what happened before the office visit) and a suspense form (what will happen at signing) for each episode.

title: The Appeal of the Mystery
venue: Journal of Aesthetics and Art Criticism
finding: Philosophical essay using the mystery, which the author calls the most widely read literary genre for more than a century, as a test case for theories of aesthetic value that must explain the lasting appeal of a kind of work.
why_for_us: Frames the micro-drama's appeal as a puzzle-solving pleasure; viewers should be able to engage cognitively with clues even in 60-90 s.

title: Cultural citizenship and crime fiction: Politics and the interpretive community
finding: Qualitative interview study with 19 readers (15 women, 4 men) of detective fiction; per the authors reading is linked to 'cultural citizenship', feminism and gender roles through interpretive communities.
why_for_us: Small but empirical: readers use crime fiction to think about civic norms; notary staff may similarly use the series to talk about professional duties, so episodes can end with a discussable point.

title: The Crime Novel
finding: Book distinguishing the crime novel from the detective story: in the detective novel a sympathetic detective solves the puzzle and restores order; in the crime novel the 'hero' is the killer, victim, guilty bystander or falsely accused, and the crime may never be satisfactorily solved.
why_for_us: Episodes told from Irena's or the son's point of view would follow the crime-novel mode (uncertainty, implication), while the notary's view gives the reassuring detective mode; the series can alternate.

title: Detecting Texts: The Metaphysical Detective Story from Poe to Postmodernism
finding: Edited volume on the 'metaphysical detective story', which ends with a question rather than an answer: the detective fails to solve the crime and confronts insoluble mysteries of interpretation and identity.
why_for_us: Shows the limit of open endings: a professional audience likely expects resolution, so ambiguity should be reserved for cliffhangers, not season endings.

title: The Perfect Murder: A Study in Detection
finding: Book drawing on British and American detective fiction to investigate why readers of all educational and social backgrounds are continually fascinated by the murder mystery.
why_for_us: Supports the assumption that the detection pleasure crosses audience groups; usable for a professional audience as well as a general one.

title: Forgers and fiction : how forgery developed the novel, 1846-79
venue: OpenGrey (Institut de l'Information Scientifique et Technique)
finding: Doctoral thesis arguing that real-life forgery cases shaped Victorian fiction: forgeries of bills, wills, parish registers and other documents appear in at least one hundred novels between 1846 and 1879 (per the author), many inspired by celebrated real cases, and forgery helped develop sensationalism.
why_for_us: Strong precedent for the season's premise: forged wills and powers of attorney drawn from real cases are a historically proven plot engine, and a document forgery story naturally fits a notary series.

title: Forgery in Nineteenth-Century Literature and Culture: Fictions of Finance from Dickens to Wilde
finding: Book on literary and cultural representations of forgery as a financial crime, from the era of mass executions of forgers in the early 19th century to the forger's emergence as a cultural figure.
why_for_us: Forgery is both a crime and a story about trust in paper; the notary's role as guarantor of authenticity makes forgery the most natural crime for the series' first season.

title: Wilkie Collins and the Inheritance Plot
finding: Doctoral thesis asking why some of the most popular mid-19th-century English novels (Collins's The Woman in White, No Name, Armadale, The Moonstone) centre on inheritance during contentious property reform and a flood of printed matter about it.
why_for_us: Inheritance and property transfer have long fuelled best-selling suspense; Irena's property sale and her son's claim belong to a proven popular plot family.

title: Esther Summerson's Narrative Relations: Re-inscribing Inheritance in Bleak House
finding: Essay arguing that in Bleak House legal discourse is evacuated of meaning through Chancery's workings and that traditional patrilineal legal inheritance is shown as unsatisfactory because it excludes female plots; Esther's telling creates a counter-narrative.
why_for_us: Bleak House is the archetypal warning against procedure that consumes people; the series should show procedure (the notary) serving the person, the reverse of Chancery.

title: The Birth of the Financial Thriller: Making a Killing in the 1970s
finding: Book tracing the financial thriller from Paul Erdman's The Billion Dollar Sure Thing (1973) against the collapse of Bretton Woods and the oil crises; analysis is organised around four aspects of the genre: theme, character, plot, and pedagogy and morality.
why_for_us: The 'pedagogy and morality' dimension matches the series' dual aim: thrill plus teaching staff what a fraudulent power of attorney or rushed sale looks like.

title: Narrating risk: the financial thriller film during the U.S. recession
finding: Essay on Margin Call (2011) and Cosmopolis (2012), arguing they revise thriller conventions by building central dramatic tension around systemic risk and financial crisis rather than conventional villainy.
why_for_us: Shows suspense can come from abstract risk (a date, a clause, a payment) if it is personalised; a deadline on a sale or a missing payment can be the 'bomb under the table'.

title: Fake It: Fictions of Forgery
finding: Book on fictions of forgery; the OpenAlex record has no abstract, so only the title and publisher are known.
why_for_us: Possible source of further forgery plots for later seasons; check content before use.

title: The Notary’s Portrait in the Mirror of World Fiction
finding: Article in a Russian notarial journal comparing images of notaries in domestic (Russian) and foreign fiction, written as a 'verbal duel'; per the author Russian literature's notaries are portrayed with clear preference and sympathy.
why_for_us: One of the few works directly on notaries in fiction; confirms that literature offers both sympathetic and unsympathetic notary portraits to position against.

title: Balzac et les notaires
venue: Le Gnomon: revue internationale d'histoire du notariat
finding: Article on notaries in Balzac in a notarial-history review; the OpenAlex record has no abstract, so only the title and venue are known.
why_for_us: Balzac's notaries are the canonical literary precedent for the profession; worth reading in full for character archetypes (the honest vs. the scheming notary).

title: Novel testaments: Balzac’s fictional wills
finding: Essay on wills in Balzac's La Comédie humaine; the record has no abstract, but its keywords list inheritance, the testator, literary stereotypes, original and copy, and counterfeit goods.
why_for_us: Confirms the will (and its copies and counterfeits) as a stock plot device in continental fiction where the notary drafts and safeguards wills.

title: Balzac's "Ursule Mirouet": Genealogy and Inheritance
finding: Essay on Balzac's Ursule Mirouët, a novel about genealogy and inheritance (relatives contesting an inheritance); the OpenAlex record has no abstract, so only the title is known.
why_for_us: Ursule Mirouët (greedy heirs vs. the intended beneficiary) is a ready literary analogue of the Irena-and-son conflict.

title: Ignorantia juris non excusat: The trial and the affirmation of the Italian legal thriller
venue: Forum Italicum A Journal of Italian Studies
finding: Essay on the rise of the Italian legal thriller and the judicial novel; per the author literary and judicial practices share methods of narrative organisation, and courtroom representation has become a prominent theme in Italian fiction.
why_for_us: Evidence that a civil-law country can develop its own legal thriller; Polish notarial practice can be the local equivalent rather than imported US courtroom imagery.

title: Legal Transplants and Legal Drama: A Comparison between the US and Italy
finding: Comparative preprint on legal drama in the US and Italy in the light of legal transplants; the OpenAlex record has no abstract, so only the title is known.
why_for_us: Relevant to the risk of importing common-law conventions into a civil-law setting; read before writing scenes that borrow US tropes.

title: Eine kleine trup, czyli dywan z wkładką. Polska powieść kryminalna – opis kilku przykładów (z sugestią teorii)
venue: Acta Universitatis Lodziensis Folia Litteraria Polonica
finding: Polish essay on the Polish crime novel, especially after 1989, asking how literary chronology depends on political change and whether those changes affected the form of the genre, as political change opened previously impossible topics.
why_for_us: Post-1989 Polish crime fiction often deals with property and transition-era themes; the series can tap the familiar Polish crime-novel register for its audience.

title: "Samobójca. Powieść karpacka" Władysława Sabowskiego: popularna powieść regionalna
venue: Acta Universitatis Lodziensis Folia Litteraria Polonica
finding: Polish essay on Sabowski's novel, regarded as the first modern Polish crime novel; per the author crime is central but there is no puzzle or path to its solution, and the sensational plot is combined with ethnographic ambitions.
why_for_us: Polish crime writing has from the start mixed crime with local colour; Polish setting and everyday office detail can be a strength, not just background.

title: Killing us softly: Investigating the aesthetics, philosophy and influence of Nordic Noir television
finding: Essay setting out Nordic Noir's narrative and aesthetic characteristics in Swedish and Danish serials (Wallander, Forbrydelsen, Broen) and arguing these techniques are designed to explore moral, social and philosophical questions.
why_for_us: Shows that a slow, sober, socially reflective style can travel internationally; a muted, realistic office aesthetic is a legitimate genre choice, not a budget compromise.

title: The Captivating Chill: Why Readers Desire Nordic Noir
finding: Essay identifying five factors behind Nordic crime fiction's international appeal: the Stieg Larsson effect, critique of the welfare state, (relative) gender equality and strong female characters, exotic landscapes and settings, and a strong link to the Anglo-American crime tradition.
why_for_us: Suggests a recipe: strong female characters (notary, Irena), a recognisably local setting, institutional critique, and familiar genre beats from the Anglo-American tradition.

title: Nordic noir in the UK: the allure of accessible difference
finding: Essay arguing that Nordic noir's UK success works as intercultural communication in which the genre's perceived 'Nordicness' negotiates social and cultural desires of the receiving culture; the author frames its appeal as 'accessible difference'.
why_for_us: 'Accessible difference' fits the series: a Polish notary office is new to genre audiences yet the genre frame keeps it legible.

title: Through Scandinavia, Darkly: A Criminological Critique of Nordic Noir
finding: Criminological essay describing Nordic noir as tied to a region, an unpretentious, socially critical narrative style and a dark aesthetic, which grew from regional niche to international phenomenon; the authors critique its account of crime.
why_for_us: Warns that social critique in crime fiction can drift into cliché; the series' critique (e.g. of family pressure on elderly owners) should stay grounded in documented cases.

title: Nordic Noir challenging ‘the language of advantage’: Setting, light and language as production values in Danish television series
finding: Essay arguing that Danish drama's UK success turned exotic settings, light, climate, language and everyday life into promotional production values rather than barriers.
why_for_us: Polish language, Polish paperwork and an ordinary office can be production values for the series, including in AI-generated imagery.

title: 〈도가니〉(황동혁, 2011)와 〈부러진 화살〉(정지영, 2012) :사회고발 매체로서의 법정영화
finding: Korean essay on the courtroom films Silenced (2011) and Unbowed (2012), fact-based films about abuse of hearing-impaired children and an individual against judicial authority, which per the author triggered public self-questioning about the Korean judicial system and disputes about their reality.
why_for_us: Korean fact-based legal films show how real cases can drive public debate, and also that they provoke disputes about accuracy; relevant to the new 'based on real cases' requirement.

title: “The rookie and the fallen elite”: an examination of the portrayal of female lawyers in the Japanese legal drama “Onna wa sore wo yurusanai”
venue: International Journal of the Legal Profession
finding: Essay finding that post-2000 Japanese legal TV dramas cast female legal professionals in two stock types with matching arcs: the rookie lawyer and the elite but 'fallen' lawyer, despite women's underrepresentation in the Japanese profession.
why_for_us: Stock character arcs travel across legal TV cultures; the series can consciously use (or subvert) the rookie-and-mentor pair for an assistant and the notary.

title: El Canon de la novela negra y policíaca. Juan José Galán Herrera.
venue: Tejuelo Didáctica de la Lengua y la Literatura Educación
finding: Spanish essay distinguishing the 'novela negra' from the 'novela problema' (puzzle novel) within detective fiction about a crime, and surveying the categories proposed for the genre.
why_for_us: Useful vocabulary for the writers' room: a 'novela problema' episode (a puzzle about a document) versus a 'negra' episode (moral murk, social pressure).

title: Moral Pluck: Legal Ethics in Popular Culture
finding: Essay arguing that favourable portrayals of lawyers in popular culture adopt a distinctive ethical perspective, 'Moral Pluck' (resourcefulness and transgression in the service of justice), which departs from the authoritarian, categorical 'elite moralism' of official bar ethics.
why_for_us: Key tension for the series: audiences love rule-bending heroes, but a notary audience needs the notary to win within the rules; resourcefulness must replace transgression.

title: When the Lawyer Knows the Client is Guilty: Client Confessions in Legal Ethics, Popular Culture, and Literature
finding: Essay on the dilemma of defence lawyers who know a client is guilty but must defend vigorously, weighing zealous representation against candour to the court via historical cases, literature and popular culture, and proposing lawyer discretion.
why_for_us: Confidentiality-vs-candour dilemmas make strong climaxes; the notarial version is what the notary may tell the son about Irena's affairs and when the notary must refuse an act.

title: ANATOMY OF HOLLYWOOD’S HERO-LAWYER: A LAW-AND-FILM STUDY OF THE WESTERN MOTIFS, HONOR-BASED VALUES AND GENDER POLITICS UNDERLYING ANATOMY OF A MURDER
venue: Studies in law, politics, and society
finding: Law-and-film essay arguing that Anatomy of a Murder (1959) borrows the Western's features, recasting the lone professional Western hero as a hero-lawyer and reviving an honour code within the law film.
why_for_us: The 'lone professional' archetype is genre-native; a notary as a calm, honour-bound professional who stands between a client and pressure fits it without courtroom heroics.

title: Lawyers, Justice and the State: The Sliding Signifier of Law in Popular Culture
finding: Semiotic essay mapping how the figure that signifies 'law' in film and TV has shifted from the heroic lawyer to the state, the police officer and the government agent, changing what 'law' means to audiences.
why_for_us: Choosing the notary as the face of law is itself a statement; the series can reclaim law's image for preventive, everyday justice rather than enforcement.

title: Trust Us Justice: 24, Popular Culture and the Law
finding: Essay arguing that the series 24, through Jack Bauer's use of torture for the common good, influenced public constructions of the relationship between the rule of law and security.
why_for_us: Popular legal fiction shapes norms; a series for notaries should model correct procedure, since 'ends justify means' heroics can leak into perceived professional norms.

title: Captured by True Crime: Why Are Women Drawn to Tales of Rape, Murder, and Serial Killers?
finding: Five studies (reader reviews, book choices, experiments manipulating story features): per the authors women are more drawn to true crime than men, whereas men prefer other violent genres, and specific features of true crime stories drive women's interest; discussed in evolutionary terms.
why_for_us: Empirical support that true-crime framing attracts audiences, notably women, who dominate notary office staff; real-case framing plus protective, practical information can be a strong hook.

title: Making a genre: the case of the contemporary true crime documentary
finding: Essay arguing that true-crime documentaries from The Staircase (2004) to Making a Murderer (2015) loosely constitute a genre sharing concerns about the law and its processes.
why_for_us: Real-case legal storytelling is an established genre; the series can borrow its devices (archival documents, dated captions, 'what the file shows') in fictionalised form.

title: Real Emotional Logic: Film and Television Docudrama as Persuasive Practice
finding: Book analysing docudrama as argument: per the author its appeal comes from representing actual people and events through melodramatic narrative structures that play on viewers' emotions, blending narrative and documentary style to argue a moral view of reality-based events.
why_for_us: Directly applicable: real cases gain persuasive power when restaged with clear emotional structure; the docudrama mode also obliges care about what is presented as fact.

title: Why docudrama? : fact-fiction on film and TV
finding: Book on fact-fiction film and TV; the abstract cites the 1990 drama Who Bombed Birmingham?, which cast doubt on the convictions of six men and preceded an inquiry that led to their release, and notes reality-based stories from topical journalism carry more influence than the average documentary.
why_for_us: Shows docudrama can have real-world legal consequences, so episodes based on court judgments must be accurate about the facts they claim and anonymise private parties.

title: America Watches "Amerika:" Television Docudrama and Political Attitudes
finding: Panel study: viewing the 1987 docudrama miniseries 'Amerika' was associated with significant attitude changes toward greater conservatism; perceived realism, education and ideology moderated effects, and indirect exposure (peer discussion, media coverage) also mattered (per the authors).
why_for_us: Empirical evidence that perceived realism amplifies docudrama effects; a 'based on real cases' label will make lessons stick, which raises the duty of accuracy.

title: Reel cruelty: Voyeurism and extra-juridical punishment in true-crime documentaries
venue: Crime Media Culture An International Journal
finding: Essay on the controversy over whether civic or pedagogical functions of true-crime documentaries outweigh harm; the authors argue trauma is not merely an unwanted by-product but bound up with voyeurism and extra-juridical punishment of real people.
why_for_us: Ethical guardrail: real perpetrators and victims must not be identifiable; fictionalise names, places and details so the series informs without punishing or exposing real people.

title: Exploring the Purposes of Fictionalization in Narrative Inquiry
finding: Methods essay identifying purposes of fictionalization in narrative inquiry, including protecting participants' identities, often required by research ethics boards to address anonymity concerns.
why_for_us: Offers a vocabulary and rationale for deliberate fictionalisation of real cases (composite characters, changed details) to protect identities while keeping the documented legal core.

title: Undisclosed Information— Serial Is My Favorite Murder : Examining Motivations in the True Crime Podcast Audience
finding: Online survey (n = 308): per the authors the true-crime podcast audience is predominantly female (73%), main motivations are entertainment, convenience and boredom, and social interaction, escape and voyeurism were significantly more salient for women.
why_for_us: Short, convenient real-case content fits the micro-drama format; social-interaction motives suggest prompts for staff to discuss each case.
